implementation_notes: TypeScript's types are erased at runtime, so an interface or type alias used as a stateless contract costs nothing, and only emitted JavaScript members count towards instance size. Multiple behaviour sources are composed with the class-expression mixin pattern (function Mixin<T extends Constructor>(Base: T) { return class extends Base { ... } }), whose methods land on the prototype and therefore add no per-instance bytes; generic constraints carry stateless policy at compile time without any runtime storage. Build each mixed class once and keep state in class fields: fields become own properties whereas methods stay shared, which is the real size lever. The classic empty base is still justified only when the emitted class must be a real extends target for framework decorators or instanceof checks.
code_sketch:
interface Clock { now(): number }                    // erased at runtime
type Ctor = new (...args: any[]) => object

const Timestamped = <T extends Ctor>(Base: T) =>
  class extends Base { stamp(): number { return Date.now(); } };  // prototype methods

class Job extends Timestamped(class { id = 0 }) {}    // id is the only own field
pitfalls: Every call of a mixin factory creates a new class object; building the mixed class per instance (or per request) breaks hidden-class sharing and can leak the class objects.
Class fields (id = 0) are per-instance own properties while methods stay on the prototype - converting a method into a field for convenience adds storage to every instance.

Interfaces and generic constraints vanish at runtime, so nothing stops a second, separately typed copy of the same stateless contract from being emitted per module, and declaration files can lose this-type information from mixin factories.
